opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I get asked quite often, and I think there's an interesting tension in it.

In principle, if you had a humanoid robot with truly human-level intelligence, it could just sit in the driver's seat and drive any car that exists today. You wouldn't need to redesign the vehicle, you wouldn't need special sensors on the roof. The robot would use the steering wheel and the pedals the same way we do. That's actually one of the core arguments for the humanoid form factor: the world is built for humans, so a general-purpose humanoid can plug into all that existing infrastructure.

But I don't think that means autonomous cars become unnecessary. Engineering-wise, a dedicated system is almost always more efficient than a general one. A self-driving car can have lidar, radar, cameras looking in every direction at once, and it never gets distracted. A humanoid sitting in the driver's seat sees through two cameras in its head, the way we do, so it inherits a lot of our limitations. Why would you build something superhuman and then constrain it to human senses for a task where you don't have to?

So my view is that they'll coexist. For high-volume, well-defined tasks like driving, specialized autonomy will win because it's safer, cheaper at scale, and easier to certify. The humanoid's real value is in the long tail: the thousands of tasks that are too diverse or too small to justify building a specialized machine for each one. Folding laundry, cooking, tidying a room, maybe even handling the edge cases around a car, like loading groceries or charging it.

And there's a deeper connection. A lot of what we learned from autonomous driving, such as large-scale data collection, simulation, and end-to-end learning, is now flowing into robotics. In a sense, self-driving cars were the first embodied AI systems deployed at scale, and humanoids are the next step on that path rather than a replacement for it.

r001.rationale: The response says a human-level humanoid could sit in the driver’s seat and drive existing cars using their controls, clearly describing it as a possible substitute for built-in autonomous driving.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun thought experiment, because it flips the usual question. People normally ask whether autonomous cars will make humanoids unnecessary for transportation, but you're asking the reverse: if we have a humanoid that's as smart as a person, do we still need to build intelligence into the car at all?

My honest answer is that in a world with a truly human-level humanoid, the dedicated autonomous car becomes much less necessary, but probably not zero. Here's the reasoning. The hard part of self-driving was never the mechanics. Steering, braking, acceleration, those were solved decades ago. The hard part is perception and decision-making in a messy, open world, with pedestrians, construction zones, weird weather, a police officer waving you through a red light. That's a general intelligence problem. If you've solved that for a humanoid, you've basically solved it for driving too, because driving is a strict subset of what a general-purpose embodied agent has to handle. So in principle, a humanoid could just sit in the driver's seat of an ordinary car and drive it, the same way a human chauffeur does. You wouldn't need to redesign every vehicle with lidar and compute and a drive-by-wire stack.

But in practice I think it still makes sense to put the intelligence in the car for a few reasons. One is sensing. A car can carry sensors a humanoid can't. Cameras at every corner, radar, 360-degree coverage. A humanoid driving with two eyes through a windshield is handicapping itself for no reason. Two is latency and reliability. Having an arm physically turn a steering wheel introduces a mechanical loop that's slower and more fragile than a direct electronic signal. If the robot's hand slips, the car crashes. Three is cost and economics. A dedicated self-driving car is doing one job, so you can specialize and optimize. Using a humanoid to drive is a bit like using a general-purpose laptop as a thermostat. It works, but it's not the elegant solution.

So where I land is something like this. The brain converges. The same foundation model, the same world model and reasoning, will probably power both the humanoid and the car. What differs is the body. For a daily commute, a fleet of robotaxis is just more efficient. But for the long tail, a humanoid carrying intelligence from one machine to another is incredibly valuable. Think about an old tractor on a farm, a forklift in a warehouse, a boat. Nobody is going to retrofit every one of those with autonomy hardware. A humanoid that can hop into any legacy machine and operate it is the bridge for all the stuff that will never get redesigned.

Actually, the part I find most exciting is not the car question at all. Once you have a humanoid with human-level intelligence, the car stops being the interesting destination. The interesting question becomes what happens at the end of the ride. Today a robotaxi drops a package at the curb and that's it. A humanoid can get out, walk up the stairs, ring the doorbell, hand it to you. Or get out and help an elderly passenger into their home. The car plus the humanoid together give you end-to-end physical autonomy, and that's a bigger change than either one alone.

r001.rationale: The response says a human-level humanoid could sit in an ordinary car and drive it, so the car would not need its own dedicated autonomous-driving system.

astra-6.text:
If we have a humanoid robot with human-level intelligence, it could get into a regular car and drive it for us. In that sense, you might not need to build autonomy into every car—you could have a robot that drives your car, then gets out and helps you carry groceries into the house.

But that doesn’t mean dedicated autonomous cars would disappear. A robot sitting in the driver’s seat might be more expensive or less efficient than a system integrated into the vehicle. And human-level intelligence alone doesn’t guarantee safe driving; the robot still needs reliable perception and physical control. So I think it creates another way to automate driving, with the choice depending on cost, safety, and how useful that robot is outside the car.

r001.rationale: The response says a human-level humanoid robot could drive a regular car, reducing the need to build autonomous driving into every car.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it changes the form of the problem, but it doesn’t make autonomous driving unnecessary. If you have a humanoid robot with human-level intelligence, you could imagine asking it to sit in the driver’s seat and drive an ordinary car. That would be useful because it could operate cars we already have.

But human-level intelligence doesn’t automatically mean it has the perception, reaction time, and reliability needed to drive safely. You still have to solve those problems. And a dedicated autonomous car may be cheaper and more efficient than putting an entire humanoid behind the wheel.

So I see them as complementary. A humanoid could drive your car, then get out and help you carry groceries. An autonomous car could focus entirely on transportation. Which approach makes sense depends on the cost and what else you want the robot to do.

r001.rationale: The response says a human-level humanoid could sit in the driver’s seat and drive an ordinary car, conveying that it could provide the driving capability instead of the car’s built-in autonomous system.
